# FEMA Export Rules 2026: EDF Filing, 9-Month Realisation Period & ₹10 Lakh EDPMS Rule


> Do you invoice clients outside India? From October 1, 2026, India's FEMA export framework has introduced new reporting requirements for service exporters, including a formal EDF process. The changes matter to freelancers, agencies, SaaS companies, software businesses, consultants and other Indian businesses serving customers overseas. This guide explains what changed, who needs to file an EDF, when export proceeds must be realised, how the ₹10 lakh EDPMS rule works, and what exporters should do now.


## RBI FEMA Export Rules 2026: Quick overview


The[Foreign Exchange Management](https://getswipe.in/blog/article/fema-compliance-common-errors) (Export and Import of Goods and Services) Regulations, 2026 bring goods, services and software under one roof. For service exporters, the headline change is the new Export Declaration Form (EDF). Export proceeds generally must be realised and repatriated within 9 months. The starting point depends on the type of export—for example, shipment date for most goods and invoice date for services. Where an export is invoiced and/or settled in Indian rupees, the applicable period is 12 months. Exports invoiced or settled in Indian rupees get 12 months.


Requirement Rule from October 1, 2026


Framework effective October 1, 2026


EDF for service exports Generally required


EDF deadline Within 30 days from the end of the invoice month


Service export realisation 9 months from invoice date


Goods export realisation 9 months from shipment date


INR-invoiced/settled exports 12 months, where applicable


Small-value EDPMS closure Up to ₹10 lakh per invoice/shipping bill


Payment tracking AD bank / EDPMS framework


At the start of the year, January 2026 regulations came into place which first set up a 15-month realisation period. RBI now amended them on September 22, 2026, just before the framework kicked in. The period dropped to 9 months, with 12 months for some specified cases.

## What changed from October 1, 2026?


The framework replaces the 2015 export regulations. Goods, services and software now sit under a single structure. For service exporters, the biggest operational shift is simple. Service exports now carry a formal EDF requirement. So if you sell an eligible service to a customer outside India, learn this chain: EDF, then payment, then EDPMS closure. This applies to many types of businesses:


- Freelancers working with overseas clients
- Digital marketing and creative agencies
- IT and software companies
- SaaS businesses
- Consultants
- BPO and support firms
- Any other Indian provider serving customers abroad

## What is an EDF under FEMA 2026?


EDF stands for Export Declaration Form. It's how you report the value of an export under the new framework. For services, you generally submit the EDF with the full export value. The deadline is 30 days from the end of the month in which you raise the invoice. One EDF can cover several service exports from the same month. Here's what an EDF may look like:


Here's an example. Say you invoice overseas clients through October 2026. You can check out[How to create an export invoice on Swipe?](https://getswipe.in/blog/product-demo/creating-an-export-invoice-on-swipe-all-cases) Your usual EDF deadline would be November 30, 2026. Non-software services get one extra option. You can file the EDF on or before the day you receive payment. Need more time? Ask your Authorised Dealer (AD) bank. It may extend the filing period if you give reasonable grounds. For services other than software, the exporter may alternatively submit the EDF on or before the date of receipt of payment.


## Who needs to file an EDF?


Indian residents who export services to overseas customers should pay attention. Some real-world cases:


- Freelancer: An Indian designer builds a brand identity for a US company.
- Agency: A marketing agency in India runs campaigns for an Australian client.
- SaaS company: An Indian software firm serves customers abroad.
- Consultant: An Indian professional advises a Singapore-based business.


Each of these can fall under the service-export framework. The exporter then needs to follow the EDF process. Software has its own wrinkle. The regulations place software within the definition of services. However, the filing route can vary with the exporter's type and location. Confirm the procedure with your AD bank or the relevant authority.


### Where do you file the EDF?


The EDF is submitted to the specified authority prescribed for the type and location of the export. For services exported from the Domestic Tariff Area, the Authorised Dealer (AD) bank is generally the relevant authority. Software exports may involve the AD bank or Software Technology Parks of India (STPI), while exports from SEZs follow the applicable SEZ reporting route. Confirm the exact filing process with your AD bank.


## Do software exporters still need to think about SOFTEX?


Yes. Software exporters should watch the transition closely. The 2026 regulations explicitly treat software as a service and bring in the EDF framework. The exact filing route may depend on whether your unit sits in the[Domestic Tariff Area](https://getswipe.in/blog/article/sez-supply-under-gst) , an[SEZ](https://getswipe.in/blog/article/sez-rules-updated-guidelines) or another setup. So don't assume your old reporting workflow still works. Check with your AD bank or the relevant authority.


## What is EDPMS?


EDPMS means[Export Data Processing and Monitoring System](https://www.icegate.gov.in/guidelines/enquiries/advisory-sb-edpms-enquiry) . Banks use it to monitor export transactions. The system tracks each one until the proceeds are realised and the entry is closed or updated. For an MSME, the workflow looks like this:


**Invoice → EDF → Overseas payment → Bank reconciliation → EDPMS closure**


Keep these records in sync. You'll avoid payment mismatches and unresolved export entries. This helps if you handle lots of small overseas transactions. Don't misread it, though. The ₹10 lakh figure isn't an exemption from export reporting. It is not an exemption from declaring or complying with the underlying export requirements. It provides a simplified mechanism for closing eligible EDPMS entries after the payment has been realised.


### What is the ₹10 Lakh EDPMS rule?


For export invoices or shipping bills up to ₹10 lakh (or the foreign-currency equivalent), the rules offer a simpler way to close the EDPMS entry. Your AD bank may close the eligible EDPMS entry based on your declaration that the payment has been realised, subject to the applicable rules and the bank's process. You can also submit that declaration quarterly for bulk closure.


## How do the new FEMA Rules affect freelancers and MSMEs?


For small exporters, the real change isn't a mountain of extra paperwork. It's the need to actively track each international invoice against its FEMA timeline. Keep a record of:


Tracking item Details to record


Invoice number & date Invoice No. / Invoice Date


Client & country Client Name / Country


Invoice value & currency Amount / Currency


EDF submission Submission date / Reference


Expected payment date Due / Expected receipt date


Actual payment receipt Date payment was received


Bank reference Bank transaction/reference number


EDPMS status Current EDPMS status


Realisation period FEMA realisation period


The more overseas clients you add, the more this habit pays off.


## What should MSMEs do now?


Build these six steps into your regular finance routine:


1. Identify your export transactions. Keep overseas service invoices apart from domestic sales.
2. Track your EDF deadline. For service invoices, it's generally 30 days after the end of the invoice month.
3. Track the realisation period separately. The EDF deadline and the realisation deadline are two different requirements.
4. Reconcile payments with invoices. Make sure your bank can match each incoming payment to the right export.
5. Monitor EDPMS closure. Getting paid doesn't automatically close every compliance entry.
6. Talk to your AD bank early. If a customer might miss the window, discuss an extension before the deadline passes.

## Conclusion


RBI's new framework brings more structure to international invoicing. If you export services, keep four numbers in mind:


- October 1, 2026: the framework takes effect
- 30 days: the general EDF filing window
- 9 months: the standard service-export realisation period
- ₹10 lakh: the simplified EDPMS closure threshold


Don't just check whether the money arrived. Follow the whole journey:


**Invoice → EDF → Payment → Bank reconciliation → EDPMS closure**


Make that your routine. Compliance gets far easier as your overseas business grows.


## FAQs


### Does FEMA apply to freelancers receiving money from foreign clients?


If you're an Indian resident serving an overseas customer, the transaction can fall under the service-export framework. Follow the applicable EDF and realisation requirements.


### What is the EDF deadline?


Generally, 30 days from the end of the month in which you raise the invoice.


### How long do I have to receive payment for a service export?


Generally, 9 months from the invoice date. Where the export is invoiced or settled in INR, you get 12 months.


### What is the ₹10 lakh rule?


For exports up to ₹10 lakh per invoice or shipping bill, you can close the EDPMS entry through a declaration confirming realisation. This is subject to the applicable rules. Quarterly bulk declarations are also allowed.


### Does the new rule create a new tax on foreign payments?


No. EDF is a foreign-exchange reporting requirement. Income tax and GST, where applicable, remain under their own laws.
